chapter_theme: The second half of Maduraikkanchi walks through one day and night of Madurai, from the day market, the shrines, the sages, the court and the crafts to the evening market, the lovers and courtesans, the festivals, the guarded watches and the dawn, then turns to the king: the spoils that feed the city, his waking among women, his honouring of warriors by merit and his open-gated giving, and ends by bidding him rejoice daily in the good time he has been given within its bound.
structure_note: The poem runs as one long chain of clauses, each description closing on a noun in -உம் (பள்ளியும், அவையமும், பகர்நரும்) or on a subject held back after a predicate in -ஏ (lines 428 to 430, 543 to 544). The core cut fell inside these descriptions in most places, so 19 of the 21 units are adjusted to the description breaks; 747-763 and 764-782 are the core units. The unit at 394 begins inside a sentence from chapter 7 and was not moved across the chapter.

pattupattu:6:394-409.reading: After the rare and great things have passed and the fear of the crowd has lifted, as at a battlefront hemmed in from both sides, the hawkers carrying many wares sit in the cool shade of mountain-like mansions: sellers of fragrant flowers in baskets, of garlands, of powder pounded by many hands, of sweet areca, long betel leaves and lime burnt from shell, and old women with white hair braided long like the white conch of the dark sea.
pattupattu:6:394-409.nuance: The unit opens inside a sentence that began in chapter 7 (the war crowd of elephants and horses in the streets); lines 402 to 404 seem to say that the townspeople who had stood in fear, as if between two enemy fronts, are released once that procession has passed, and only then does the market settle. What the drum-head simile of lines 395 and 396 is compared to is not fixed by the text.
pattupattu:6:394-409.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 394-411: the old women's description closes at தொன்முது பெண்டிர் in line 409, and line 410 begins the young women (செந்நீர்ப் பசும்பொன் புனைந்த பாவை). The start at 394 is the chapter boundary and stays, though the sentence began in chapter 7.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the king's city by describing it, which is paadaan matter inside the kaanchi frame

comparisons.tenor: the round loads (or baskets) of the hawkers, on one reading
the crowd hemmed in on both sides, who sighed in fear for their lives
the old women's long white braids

pattupattu:6:410-430.reading: Young women glowing like a golden doll in the tender light of the setting sun, with wounding glances, dark skin, slipping armlets, painted young breasts and hair thick as spilled kohl, some with a peacock's gait and some with soft speech, walk gently, clap and laugh and play with unlettered men, and carry their wares in decorated caskets with fragrant flowers from house to house; and the din of the wide day market of Koodal, never lessened by what is taken nor swollen by what is brought, like the sea that clouds drink from and rivers pour into, rose like a land in festival on the evening of the seventh day.
pattupattu:6:410-430.nuance: The sea simile (lines 424 to 426) is built as a double balance: the sea keeps its level because what the clouds take and what the rivers bring cancel out, and the market keeps its plenty because taking and bringing go on together. The sentence's subject, the din of the day market, is held back until after its verb ஆர்த்தன்றே, the same pattern the poet uses for the evening market at line 544.
pattupattu:6:410-430.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 394-411, 412-428 and 429-441: the young women begin at line 410, and the sentence closing in ஆர்த்தன்றே (line 428) names its subject, the din of Koodal's day market, in lines 429 and 430.

pattupattu:6:431-452.reading: Rich lords of cloud-like generous hands, in bright cloth red as the evening glow tied with gold-hilted swords, garlands like strung gems on their adorned chests, drive horses swift as the wind with runners guarding them; and to watch their daily pleasure, women with gold anklets and bright bangles, fair as goddesses come down, fill the street with fragrance, their bright faces appearing and vanishing like the moon among clouds on the terraces of tiered mansions, between banners that wave like the waves of the clear sea.
pattupattu:6:431-452.nuance: The rich men are seen through the eyes of the women who come to look at them (காண்மார், line 443), so the street scene is doubled: display below, watching above. The moon among clouds (line 452) catches the women's faces as they show and hide behind the moving banners.
pattupattu:6:431-452.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 429-441, 442-453: the description of the riders begins at line 431 after the day-market sentence closes at 430, and the women's faces of line 448 come to rest at மறைய in line 452; line 453 begins the five elements of the god who heads the temple.

pattupattu:6:453-467.reading: With the axe-bearing tall one, who made water, earth, fire, wind and the great sky together, at their head, the gods of spotless shining bodies, unfading flowers, unblinking eyes and food of fragrance receive high offerings of unchanging custom at the evening festival with drums; and mature women holding little boys in bright pendants, as one holds a pollen-filled lotus bud, shining together with them, worship with flowers and incense at the gods' shrine that guards the city from outside.
pattupattu:6:453-467.nuance: The god who made the five elements is named only by his axe (மழு) and his height (நெடியோன்); the text does not settle which god is meant. The gods' marks in lines 456 to 458 (no blinking, flowers that do not fade, food that is only fragrance) are the standard signs that distinguish gods from men.
pattupattu:6:453-467.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 442-453, 454-471: the list of the five elements begins at line 453, and the shrine's description closes on the noun கடவுட் பள்ளியும் in line 467; line 468 begins the Brahmins' Veda.

pattupattu:6:468-488.reading: Next the Brahmins' dwelling, like a hill carved out, where great ones of loving heart live at ease, singing the Veda, keeping a conduct of high merit, unique in this world and reaching the higher world from here without straying from the path of right; and the fragrant flowered dwelling of the sages, praised with flowers and incense by the lay followers (சாவகர்), where knowers who understand past and coming time and the present and know sky and earth whole, of unbending body and restrained, crowd in to keep their fasts, with water pots hung in slings of twisted cord, high red walls like copper rising beyond sight, the place shining like many hills gathered together.
pattupattu:6:468-488.nuance: Two religious houses are set side by side: the Brahmins, marked by Veda and rite but also by a loving heart (அன்புடை நெஞ்சு, line 472), and a community of ascetics whose lay followers are called சாவகர் and who know past, present and future. The text names their practices (fasting, water pots in slings) but not their sect; that they are Jain or Buddhist is an inference.
pattupattu:6:468-488.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 454-471, 472-492: the Brahmins' description begins at சிறந்த வேதம் in line 468, and the sages' dwelling closes at line 488 (குன்றுபல குழீஇப் பொலிவன தோன்ற), before the court of justice in line 489.

pattupattu:6:489-506.reading: Then the court that speaks right, which puts away fear, grief and desire, and keeps from both hatred and delight, being straight like the beam of a balance; the kaviti officers with sandal on their chests, who like the great ones who move in the sky examine good and evil and restrain them, keep love and right, shun blame and are full of fame; and the merchants who never stray from right, in many-roomed houses like a cluster of hills where kites perch and fly, rich with goods and food, selling things of hill, land and water and gems, pearls and gold from excellent countries.
pattupattu:6:489-506.nuance: Lines 489 and 490 list exactly what the judges must set aside: three feelings that bend a judgment by weakness (fear, grief, desire) and two that bend it by partisanship (hatred, delight). The balance word ஞெமன் is the one Purananuru 6 uses for the same image.
pattupattu:6:489-506.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 472-492, 493-509: the court begins at line 489 (அச்சமும் அவலமும்), and the merchants' clause closes on பகர்நரும் in line 506; line 507 begins the simile of Pazhaiyan's Mohur.

pattupattu:6:507-526.reading: Like the four-tongued Kosar appearing at the assembly of Pazhaiyan's Mohur, a town of rain that never fails and harvests that never fail, the four great groups appear; and shell cutters, gem borers, goldsmiths, gold assayers, cloth sellers, weighers of copper, bundle tiers, those who choose flowers and incense, and painters of keen sight who can show any work in images, small and great craftsmen together, spread their goods short and long like the ripples of a clear wave and stand in all four streets, with a clamour like the eager din of the great day's assembly of the cool-sea lord, whom drum-beating kodiyar bless with their families.
pattupattu:6:507-526.nuance: The poet measures Madurai's assembly against another lord's: the four-tongued Kosar at Pazhaiyan's Mohur, a vassal court. Which the four groups are is not said. The trades of lines 511 to 518 are a catalogue of the city's crafts, ending with the painter, whose work is to 'show every work by likeness' (எவ்வகைச் செய்தியும் உவமங் காட்டி).
pattupattu:6:507-526.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 493-509, 510-527: the Kosar simile begins at line 507 and completes at நாற்பெருங் குழுவும் in line 510, and the craftsmen's clamour closes at கடுப்ப in line 526; line 527 begins the list of foods.

comparisons.tenor: the four great groups appearing in Madurai
the goods spread out short and long

pattupattu:6:527-544.reading: Fragrant sap, jackfruit segments, sweet mangoes of rare beauty, vegetables and fruits of many shapes, tender greens with their buds loosed, grown by the east wind's rain, pieces of sweet cane like nectar, famous rice with meat, tubers that grow downward and the rest are eaten everywhere from those who serve sweet rice; and, like the roar of the port where wind-driven ships with white sails unload many goods, or the cries of many birds that rise at midnight when the flood of the great sea pours into the backwaters, there spills the clamour of the evening market.
pattupattu:6:527-544.nuance: As at line 430, the subject (the din of the evening market) comes after the predicate, so the two markets of Madurai, the day market (நாளங்காடி) and the evening market (அல்லங்காடி), each end a long period on the word கம்பலை. The noise is twice compared to the sea: the port, and the tide flooding the backwaters at midnight.
pattupattu:6:527-544.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 510-527, 528-543, 544-559: the list of foods begins at சேறு நாற்றமும் in line 527, and the sentence ending in இசையெழுந் தற்றே (line 543) names its subject, the evening market's clamour, in line 544.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the king's city by describing it, which is paadaan matter inside the kaanchi frame

comparisons.tenor: the sweet cane pieces
the noise of the workers moving with their wares
the clamour of the evening market

pattupattu:6:545-561.reading: The sun, its burning light dimmed and its anger cooled, takes the good day with it to the western hill; from the east the full moon rises and night comes wearing the look of day; women who long to join their dear partners string cool water-lilies, put on jewels, perfume their long hair, grind narantham, stir sandal and smoke their soft clothes; doe-eyed women glad in their womanhood light tall lamps; love-sickness enters every part of the great city as the noisy evening departs; and, tuning the seven-stringed small lute to a changed mode, they embrace the partners they desire, so that the wide sky is fragrant.
pattupattu:6:545-561.nuance: This is akam matter (lovers making ready for union at nightfall) carried inside a puram poem's tour of the city, so the love-sickness (நோய், line 557) is not one woman's but the whole city's. Line 549 makes the moonlit night 'take on the form of day', which is why the city can keep moving. The vehicle of the simile in line 560 (தாழ்பயல்) is not clear to us.
pattupattu:6:545-561.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 544-559, 560-576: the evening begins at line 545 after the evening market's clamour closes at 544, and the householders' union closes with வீழ்துணை தழீஇ வியல்விசும்பு கமழ in line 561; line 562 begins the courtesans.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening of the lovers is one hour of the city's day in a description that praises the city

comparisons.tenor: the women's glances
the tone of the lute as they change its mode

pattupattu:6:562-589.reading: The courtesans throw off garlands bright as gathered water, swing their bright bangles, fill the street with the scent of fresh flowers, deck themselves like a flowering bush in the rains, embrace until their ornaments scar the chest, weave many deceiving lies and hide their true embrace, and draw in the many rich young men who came from far and near for their beauty until their wealth is spent, then leave them as soft-winged bees drink the pollen and abandon the empty flower; and like fruit-seeking birds the wealthy householders and others come to their fine houses, where women in bright bangles crowd under lamps like celestial women dancing in the blue sky, kondi women who make onlookers' hearts tremble, dance to the drum amid the midnight lute, and, tired of the sand of the cold ford, pluck tender sprays, put on long-stalked water-lilies and play at poythal in every fragrant house.
pattupattu:6:562-589.nuance: The poet names the deceit outright (மாயப் பொய்பல, line 570) and the draining of wealth (வளந்தப வாங்கி, line 572), and gives the men two images that are not flattering, the bee at an empty flower and the bird that lives by seeking fruit; but the scene stays inside the praise of the city. கொண்டி (line 583) elsewhere means plunder, so these may be women brought in from conquered lands.
pattupattu:6:562-589.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 560-576, 577-592: the courtesans begin at நீர்திரண் டன்ன கோதை in line 562, and their night closes on பொய்தல் அயர in line 589; line 590 begins the Onam festival.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesans' night is part of the city's catalogue of pleasures, not one lover's situation

comparisons.tenor: the bright garlands the women cast off
the fragrance of the women
the women decked in flowers

comparisons.vehicle: நுண்தா துண்டு வறும்பூத் துறக்கும் மென்சிறை வண்டின மான
comparisons.tenor: the courtesans who drain the young men's wealth and leave them

comparisons.tenor: the women crowding and dancing under the lamps

pattupattu:6:590-603.reading: On the good day of Onam, the feast of Mayon of the golden garland who overcame the hosts of asuras, warriors of the fighting quarter, faces and foreheads scarred from unyielding battle, hands that bear the fight, wearing garlands full of bees, eager for combat, drive fierce elephants at each other in mock battle so that the cloths the watchers spread are strewn on the ground, and roam drunk on strong toddy; and women of rich houses who have borne sons to their husbands' joy, milk flowing from their young breasts, the smell of childbirth gone, bathe in the tank with their shining kin.
pattupattu:6:590-603.nuance: Lines 592 to 598 are hard: what scarred the warriors' faces (கோணம், சாணம்) and what the watchers threw on the shore (காழகம்) we read only tentatively. The festival joins two kinds of strength the city honours, the scarred warrior and the mother newly risen from childbirth.
pattupattu:6:590-603.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 577-592, 593-615: Onam begins at line 590 with Mayon's victory, and the new mothers' bath closes at குளநீர் அயர in line 603; line 604 begins the lute and the pregnant women's worship.

pattupattu:6:604-619.reading: Setting the frets and tuning the sevvazhi mode, the lute joined with the drum and the small aguli beating, lamps going ahead with the offerings, pregnant women moving gently like peacocks worship with joined hands while the broad-shouldered priestess gives them the offering; on one side the velan of strict rites surrounds them with Murugan's presence to the sound of sweet instruments, and wearing kurinji flowers of the rainy season and kadamba they honour the tall Vel and dance the kuravai hand in hand in every square; in every quarter speech, song and dance mingle, many separate clamours whirl in frenzy, like the roar of the street festival in the land of Nannan of great fame.
pattupattu:6:604-619.nuance: The hill god's rite has come into the city: the kurinji flower (a thing of another land, line 613) is worn in Madurai's squares. The priestess (சாலினி) and the velan serve women at a life crisis, pregnancy, which suggests what the Murugan rite was used for in town.
pattupattu:6:604-619.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 593-615, 616-631: the lute and the pregnant women's worship begin at line 604, and the festival's mingled noise closes at ஆர்ப்பெழுந் தாங்கு in line 619; line 620 begins the passing of the first watch.

comparisons.tenor: the pregnant women's gentle walk
the mingled clamour of every quarter of Madurai

pattupattu:6:620-631.reading: When the first watch of night has gone, the conch's noise dies down, the traders lower their bars and shut their long shop doors, young women bright in jewels go to bed, the sweet-makers who sell soft cakes like fine-lined honeycomb, sugar shaped like fine sand and carefully folded modakam doze and sleep, the dancers of the festival lie still, and, like the cold sea when its roar has ceased, those on their beds sleep sweetly in the depth of midnight.
pattupattu:6:620-631.nuance: The city that roared like the sea by day (lines 424 to 426, 536 to 543) is now the sea with its roar ceased; the poet keeps one image for Madurai across the whole day.
pattupattu:6:620-631.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 616-631: the first watch begins at line 620 after the festival's clamour closes at 619; the unit ends at the core boundary, midnight (கங்குல் இடையது, line 631).

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the king's city by describing it, which is paadaan matter inside the kaanchi frame

comparisons.tenor: the soft cakes
the city fallen asleep

pattupattu:6:632-653.reading: In that midnight, ghosts and spirits take on forms and roam with Death of the killing chariot and the demons, and in darkness thick as the hide of a black she-elephant, thieves go about seeking jewels, with swords that cut stone and wood, leather on their feet, short daggers at the thigh, blue belts, rope ladders of soft thread and chisels that dig through earth; but the town's guards, who track the hiding places of these men, sleepless like a strong tiger watching a strong elephant, fearless, praised for their manhood, never straying from the treatise and keen in judgment, with arrows none can escape, rise tirelessly and walk the streets through the half night of rain, when water runs in the chariot streets and the gods themselves walk, so that the last watch passes safe and without fear until day.
pattupattu:6:632-653.nuance: The thieves' kit is listed as closely as the craftsmen's tools by day (lines 511 to 518): night too has its trades. The guards are praised as men who keep to the treatise (நூல்வழிப் பிழையா, line 646), so watch-keeping is a learned craft, not only courage.
pattupattu:6:632-653.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 632-649, 650-665: the guards' patrol, begun at line 642, completes at line 653, where the last watch passes 'safe, without fear' (அச்ச மறியா தேம மாகிய மற்றை யாமம் பகலுறக் கழிப்பி); line 654 begins the dawn.

thinai_evidence.note: the guarded night shows the king's protection of his city

comparisons.tenor: the thick darkness of midnight
the sleepless town guards watching for thieves

pattupattu:6:654-667.reading: At dawn, like the bee that drinks pollen humming at the bud in a fragrant pond whose flowers have loosed their bonds, the Brahmins who recite chant the Veda; lute players tune the strings sweetly and play the marutham mode; mahouts feed balls of food to the fierce elephants; the stabled horses of the tall chariots are sated with grass; the shops of many wares are washed with dung; the toddy sellers call out their drink; and wives who slept in their loving husbands' arms, wanting the spreading dawn, walk with their bright gold jewels ringing, like streaks of lightning that dazzle the eye, and the doors of the strong-walled houses creak open.
pattupattu:6:654-667.nuance: The lute players' mode is marutham, the mode of the landscape whose hour, by porul 1.9, is dawn; the music keeps the time-scheme of akam even in a city poem.
pattupattu:6:654-667.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 650-665, 666-681: the dawn begins at line 654 after the last watch passes at 653, and the wives' rising closes with the creaking doors at கதவங் கரைய in line 667; line 668 begins the drunken old warriors.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the king's city by describing it, which is paadaan matter inside the kaanchi frame

comparisons.tenor: the Brahmins chanting the Veda
the wives moving in bright gold jewels

pattupattu:6:668-686.reading: Old warriors whose tongues lisp with drink raise their roaring voices; the sootar praise, the magadhar recite and the vaitalikar announce the hours; the sounding drum resounds and bulls bellow in answer; the spotted cock crows at daybreak; the heron with its mate and the lovely swan cry, the peacock calls, the great tusker with its cow trumpets, the caged beast roars with the tiger; and women of fine jewels, like lightning leaping in a sky cleared of cloud, who sulked over their wine and tore their thick necklaces, have the scattered pearls, the fallen young fruits and the soft faded flowers swept from the sanded courtyards where bees hum, at the safe dawn when night departs.
pattupattu:6:668-686.nuance: The dawn is told entirely by sound: men (warriors, bards, heralds), then drum and bull, then birds, then beasts. The women's sulking over wine (புலந்தனர், line 680) is akam's oodal, glimpsed only by its litter. Lines 682 and 683 (the 'fire that melts gold' simile and the young fruits) we cannot fix.
pattupattu:6:668-686.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 666-681, 682-695: the drunken warriors begin at line 668 after the doors creak at 667, and the sweeping of the courtyards closes on இரவுத்தலைப் பெயரு மேம வைகறை in line 686; line 687 begins the spoils of war.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the king's city by describing it, which is paadaan matter inside the kaanchi frame

comparisons.tenor: the jewelled women
something scattered in the courtyard, perhaps the fallen fruits

pattupattu:6:687-699.reading: Tuskers left behind in the middle ground when the dark-shouldered mazhavar were routed, leaping horses seized in enemy country, herds that the fierce kooliyar, cutting men down with the spear as their goad, brought back by the light of burning towns, and all the precious things that came from every land, worshipped daily at the guarded gate of the good fort, pour into Madurai of great name with immeasurable wealth, like the great Ganges spreading into the sea, so that it shines like the gods' world and has surpassing fame.
pattupattu:6:687-699.nuance: The wealth of the markets has a source, and this unit names it: elephants left on the field, horses taken, herds driven home by the light of burning towns. The 'burning towns' (ஊர்சுடு) are what the Purananuru's raid poems celebrate; here they are the start of a flow that ends in the city's splendour. What the அணங்குடைத் தோட்டி of line 693 is (a guarded gate, a goad hung as an emblem) we read tentatively.
pattupattu:6:687-699.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 682-695, 696-711: the spoils begin at line 687 after the dawn closes at 686, and the sentence closes on its subject, பெரும்பெயர் மதுரை, in line 699; line 700 begins the women in the grove.

thinai_evidence.note: what the unit describes is plunder taken in raids on enemy land, which is vanji

comparisons.tenor: the spear used as a goad to drive the captured herds
the spoils of every land flowing into Madurai

pattupattu:6:700-724.reading: In a grove where the ashoka's bright flowers, red as fire and humming with bees, have opened on every branch, you embraced the fragrant shoulders of women whose gold jewels shine like the young sunlight of the rising sun, with a peacock's gentle grace, skin like mango shoots, freckles on their backs, bright earrings in their ears and faces like the great pollen-laden lotus of the god's pond, and slept on a bed bright with garlands; then, rising sweetly when good sleep left you, you rubbed sandal on your chest hung with bright pearl strings, the bee-swarmed garland hanging to your neck, gold armlets shining on your strong hands, starched cloth wrapped as your dress, and stood in a form like Murugan's, like a painted figure made by a master.
pattupattu:6:700-724.nuance: Here the poem turns from the city to the king and from the third person to 'you' (நின், line 727, and the second-person உருவினை யாகி, line 724). His waking repeats the city's: Madurai woke to sounds and opened doors, the king wakes from his women's arms and is dressed, so the ruler's day is told as one more part of the city's day.
pattupattu:6:700-724.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 696-711, 712-727: the grove of women begins at line 700 after the sentence about Madurai closes at 699, and the king's dressing closes on முருகியன் றன்ன உருவினை யாகி in line 724; line 725 begins the warriors' praise.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's night and waking are described to praise him

pattupattu:6:725-746.reading: Warriors eager for battle, who cut through and routed the enemy like a stone dam that stops a flood, praise the victory of your feet joined with the sword's wealth; and the strong-armed warriors whose chests took arrows round the bow, the lords who strove at strong forts with stone-cut moats, the chiefs who fell nobly where great elephants fell in battle amid an army like rising flame and drums of unscraped bull hide sounded ceaselessly, and those of worn chests like a strong hub, armour split by spears and arrows, who did not slacken in high service, and the men of great deeds who captured herds of tall elephants: on the worthy you set the golden thumbai, not asking who they are but weighing their order of merit.
pattupattu:6:725-746.nuance: Line 738 is the hinge: the king crowns the worthy 'without saying who are you' (நீர்யார் என்னாது) and 'considering order' (முறைகருதுபு). Honour goes by the order of deeds just listed (arrows taken, forts stormed, elephants captured), not by birth.
pattupattu:6:725-746.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 712-727, 728-746: the warriors' praise begins with the stone-dam simile at line 725 after the king's dressing closes at 724; the unit ends at the core boundary, line 746.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's honouring of warriors by their deeds is vaakai, the celebration of excellence

comparisons.tenor: the warriors who stopped and routed the enemy

pattupattu:6:747-763.reading: 'Let all come, and bring the others too,' you say, sitting without anger at a gate that is never barred, 'let the bards come, let the women singers come, let the new poets come with the dancers', and to all the suppliants who support large families you give tall chariots with kodinji and elephants; in every yard toddy is strained, at every tree post rams are felled, fat meat roasts and melts, ghee boils and frying sizzles, and the smoke of seasoning spreads like rain mist so the wide city cannot be seen; like the Tall One of land-giving fortune who, with the good teachers of ancient command trained in the sacrificial rites of Mudukudumi of many halls, ate the shared feast.
pattupattu:6:747-763.nuance: The king is measured against the dynasty's past: the feast is like that of a Tall One (நெடியோன்) who ate with the teachers of Mudukudumi's sacrifices. Whether this நெடியோன் is an earlier Pandya or the god is not settled by the line. Line 761 (தொல்லாணை நல்லாசிரியர்) recurs in Pattinappalai 170, a shared formula for the Vedic teachers.

thinai_evidence.note: the open gate and the feast praise the king's giving

comparisons.tenor: the smoke of the cooking that hides the city

pattupattu:6:764-782.reading: Worthy in wonder, nobility and rectitude, flawless in the praise of many mouths, bringing rare things and widening your people, learning great things and spreading fame, shining sweetly with flourishing kin like the sun amid the sea and the moon amid many stars, while the young Kosar of victorious true swords, with Maran of great name and unfailing fame at their head, listen to your true word of ordered custom, and the chieftains of great valour, the five of golden ornaments among them, crowd in and praise you in your assembly of shining fame, and bright-jewelled women pour fragrant wine from golden vessels: rejoice and live sweetly every day, great one, in the good span of time you have been given within its bound.
pattupattu:6:764-782.nuance: The poem's last word sets the whole description in its kaanchi frame: the good time is one 'you got within a bound' (வரைந்து நீ பெற்ற, line 782), so the closing 'rejoice every day' is counsel given in view of its end, not only a blessing. The formula 'with X at the head' (மாறன் தலைவனாக, line 772) also opens the list of praising chiefs, as in Purananuru 72.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing counsel speaks of a bounded span of good time, the kaanchi matter of the colophon

comparisons.tenor: the king amid his kin

links.note: The idyll's sea keeps its level because what the clouds take and what the rivers bring balance; the Kural says the vast sea itself would lose its nature if the cloud took and did not give back.
links.teaches: The sea's unchanging fullness was a stock figure of plenty in the city poem, and the Kural takes the same sea to show that the fullness depends on the return, which, read back into the market, makes Madurai's inexhaustible plenty the effect of continual exchange rather than a fixed store.

links.note: The idyll's அந்தணர் are marked by Veda, rite and high conduct, and only in passing by a loving heart; the Kural says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous because they are kind to every creature.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows the Kural keeping the idyll's name but moving its definition from the Veda and the rite to the one trait the idyll mentions last, kindness, so the couplet reads as a deliberate redefinition of a status the court poem took for granted.

links.note: Purananuru 6 wishes the Pandya Mudukudumi to lean to no side like the beam of a balance (ஞமன்); the idyll gives the same balance (ஞெமன்கோல்) to Madurai's court of justice, which puts away fear, grief, desire, hatred and delight.
links.teaches: The impartiality that the earlier poem asks of the king in person has, in Nedunjeliyan's Madurai, become the work of an institution, and the idyll spells out the five passions the court must set aside, which the wish to the king left unnamed.

links.note: The Kural's worthy man is like the balance that first levels itself and then weighs; the idyll's court is straight like the balance once it has put away fear, grief, desire, hatred and delight.
links.teaches: The idyll's list says what the Kural's 'first making itself level' consists of, the clearing of five named passions before judgment, so the couplet's compressed image can be unpacked from a description of a working court.

links.note: The idyll names the courtesans' many deceiving lies and hidden embraces and their draining of rich young men, but lists them among the splendours of the city; the Kural likens the false embrace of women who sell themselves to embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room.
links.teaches: The deceit the Kural turns into horror was already admitted, in the same terms of lying and false embrace, by the court poet, who still counted it as part of the city's wealth, so the moralist's chapter answers a practice that praise poetry had treated as a sign of prosperity.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's veri ground and the festivals of every town among the places where Murugan is found; the idyll shows the velan and a priestess at work in Madurai's squares, serving pregnant women, with kurinji and kadamba worn in the city.
links.teaches: The guide poem gives the rite's places and the city poem gives its users, so together they show the hill god's veri carried into the capital and used for women's life crises such as pregnancy, which neither poem states alone.

links.note: Kalladanar shows Nedunjeliyan's work in enemy country: fouled fords, plundered fields, felled guarded trees, burned houses, an empty waste; the idyll shows tuskers, horses and herds brought by the light of burning towns flowing into Madurai like the Ganges into the sea.
links.teaches: The two poems are the two ends of one process under the same king: the ruin praised in the Purananuru is the source of the abundance praised in Maduraikkanchi, so the city's splendour is the enemy land's emptiness moved to the capital.

links.note: The Kural says many will live by a king who looks at people not alike but by rank (வரிசை); the idyll's king crowns warriors with the gold thumbai 'not asking who they are' but weighing their order (முறைகருதுபு), after listing the deeds that rank them.
links.teaches: The idyll shows a ceremony in which the king's ranking goes by deeds rather than by birth, which supports reading the Kural's வரிசை as an order of merit and shows what the couplet's 'many will live looking to it' meant in practice for a warrior following.

links.note: In Purananuru 72 Nedunjeliyan stakes his vow on the poverty of not giving to suppliants; the idyll shows his gate never barred, bards, singers and poets called in, and chariots and elephants given.
links.teaches: Read together, the open-gate scene is the vow's condition kept: what the young king named as the shame he would accept if he failed (not being able to give) is what the poet, in the king's own lifetime, presents as his settled daily practice.

links.note: Purananuru 15 addresses Mudukudumi himself, asking whether his enemies or his completed Vedic sacrifices are more; the idyll measures Nedunjeliyan's feast against one shared with the teachers trained in the sacrifices of Mudukudumi of many halls.
links.teaches: The sacrifices that Purananuru 15 praises as one king's deeds had become, by Nedunjeliyan's time, an inherited institution with its own line of teachers, and the standard against which a later Pandya's liberality was measured.

links.note: Nedunjeliyan vows that if he fails, poets with Mangudi Maruthan at their head may cease to sing his land; the idyll, by Mangudi Maruthanar, ends with chiefs with Maran at their head praising him in assembly.
links.teaches: The vow names the poet whose song was at stake, and the idyll is that poet's song, ending in a praise-assembly built on the same 'X at the head' formula, so the pair shows the poet answering the king's vow in kind while closing, as kaanchi, on the bound of the king's good time.

links.note: Purananuru 6 ends by wishing Mudukudumi to last on earth like the cool moon and the burning sun; the idyll uses the same pair to show Nedunjeliyan shining among his kin, then closes on the good time he has been given within a bound.
links.teaches: The kaanchi poet takes the dynasty's formula of sun and moon but uses it for brightness among kin, not for duration, and pointedly ends on the limit of the span, so the closing withholds exactly the wish for lastingness that the praise poem gave.

links.note: Naladiyar 6 starts from the appointed span of days and concludes: give your wealth away, for tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; the idyll starts from the good time given within a bound and concludes: rejoice and live sweetly every day.
links.teaches: Both counsels rest on the same premise of a fixed span, but the idyll, after showing the king's giving, lets pleasure stand beside it as a right answer, while the ethics book allows only giving, so the later text narrows a kaanchi argument that once had room for enjoyment.

source_issues: Line 662: our text reads களிதொடை (the toddy sellers' 'intoxicating strings'?), the flagged tvu reading is களிநொடை, 'selling' (நொடை, as at line 622 நொடைநவில்); the tvu reading fits the toddy sellers' calling out better. Our reading is kept in the marks.

Lines 753 to 761 print the short lines with word-internal spaces (கள் ளரிப்ப, மை வீழ்ப்ப, தொல் லாணை நல் லாசிரியர்); line 761 is the same as Pattinappalai 170 (தொல்லாணை நல்லாசிரியர்), where it is printed without the spaces. Karu forms are taken from the spaced text.

Lines 776 and 777 split one word across the line break (மன்ன / ரவரும், for மன்னர் அவரும்), and பிறகும் in line 777 looks like a misprint for பிறரும் ('and others'), matching பிறரும் in lines 518, 577 and 746.
Line 682 (பொன்சுடு நெருப்பி னிலமுக் கென்ன) is unclear to us; நிலமுக்கு may be a corrupt or rare word.
Line 394 begins inside a sentence that started in chapter 7 (the crowd of elephants, chariots and horses, lines 380 to 393); the chapter boundary was not moved.
